newsitem.title: ITALY: Anglican archbishop arrives in Rome to meet Pope.
newsitem.headline: Anglican archbishop arrives in Rome to meet Pope.

text.p: The Archbishop of Canterbury George Carey arrived in Italy on Tuesday to meet Pope John Paul and discuss relations between the Anglican and Catholic churches, including differences over women priests and papal authority.

Carey and his entourage, including his wife Eileen, arrived at Rome's Fiumicino airport from London. Carey, spiritual leader of the world's 70 million Anglicans, declined to answer questions from reporters.
He was due to have a first meeting with the Pontiff later on Tuesday (1730 GMT) ahead of substantive talks with the Pope on Thursday in an official audience at the Vatican.

Carey, who had an unofficial meeting with the Pope during a visit to Italy in May 1992, was also due on Tuesday to preach at the American Episcopal Church of St Paul's Within the Walls, where Rome's first Anglican woman priest was recently ordained.

Carey and the conservative, ailing, 76-year-old Pope, now in the 19th year of his pontificate, are expected to stress their commitment to eventual unity between the Churches which split in 1534 when King Henry VIII refused to accept papal authority.
That issue -- recognition of the Pope's supreme authority over any unified Christian church -- is still an obstacle more than 450 years later.

In a move with potentially historic consequences, the Pope said in a 1995 encyclical that, for the sake of unity, he was willing to seek an accommodation with other Christian denominations on the future role of the papacy.
But he made clear he would not accept a symbolic papacy without teeth and that Rome would have to hold the primary place among Christians because St Peter, the first Pope, died there.
The Pope reiterated the position in remarks on Monday.

"For non-Catholic Christianity, the Roman primate (the Pope) is a permanent, obvious challenge towards a concrete unity," the Pope said. He added however that the papacy was "the duty of the Church and...should be its recognisable sign before the world".
The question of women priests has also proved a sticking point during some 30 years of Anglican-Catholic dialogue.
In 1994, the Church of England, mother Church of the Anglican Communion, began ordaining women. The Vatican has a strict ban on women priests.

In 1995 the Vatican said the Catholic ban on female ordination was a definitive, infallible and unquestionable part of Church doctrine. The ruling would make it difficult if not impossible for a future Pope to change the ruling for some time.

The Catholic Church says it does not have the authority to allow women to become priests because Christ, in a free and sovereign way, chose only men as his apostles and was therefore reflecting "divine will".
